Onerous

OH-nur-us -- from Latin onus, 'burden, load': something onerous weighs on you like a heavy load. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Onerous is oppressively burdensome.

Grading two hundred essays over a single weekend felt like the most onerous part of the teacher's entire year.

Worked Example

What should have been a simple oil change turned into an entire Saturday spent removing rusted bolts one stubborn quarter-turn at a time.

Onerous describes a burden that's heavier or more draining than it should be -- a routine oil change becoming an entire lost Saturday is exactly the kind of unwelcome weight the word captures.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

taxing: demanding a great deal of effort or energy

oppressive: difficult to bear, in a harsh or overwhelming way

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

effortless: requiring little or no effort

light: easy to carry or bear

Where it sits · how crushing the load feels — taxing → onerous → oppressive

taxing vs. onerous: Taxing describes any draining effort, even a fairly ordinary one, while onerous adds the sense that the burden is unfair or excessive for what it should be.

oppressive vs. onerous: Oppressive goes further than onerous, suggesting a burden so harsh or overwhelming it feels almost crushing, not just tiring.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — oner

Root — oner: burden, load (the stem of Latin onus, 'burden')

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of, having the quality of (Latin -osus)

Put it together

Put it together: Oner ('burden, load' — the stem of Latin onus) + -ous ('full of'): something onerous is, quite literally, full of burden — the same root behind the word exonerate, 'to take the burden off.'

Use the root in a new word: exonerate

Use the root in a new word: exonerate: New DNA evidence finally exonerated the man after he had spent a decade in prison.

Root Check

Word Choice

Onerous most often describes tasks, duties, or responsibilities -- it is rarely used to describe people directly.
